title: NVIDIA Q1/26 - Cash & Marketable Securities
subtitle: Treasury vs FP&A: one balance, two ways of reading it
openingQuestion: What do Treasury and FP&A each look at cash & marketable securities for?
openingOptions: One side wants to borrow more, and the other to set the dividend
One optimises liquidity, the other optimises capital strategy
There is no real difference between the two functions
Purely as decoration on the published financial statements
explanation: Treasury looks at liquidity and short-term risk; FP&A looks at how the cash should be used for buybacks, M&A, capex or reserves. Both functions look at the same cash figure on the balance sheet but ask very different questions of it: is this safe enough yet, versus how should it be allocated to create the most value.

realWorldExample.description: A fast-growing business may hold a large cash pile to balance investment, buybacks and a buffer against the cycle.

quiz.question: Is a large cash balance on the balance sheet always a bad sign?
options: Yes, a large cash pile is always capital going to waste
No, and the cash balance has never mattered anyway
No, provided it comes with a clear capital strategy
It is only bad at companies in the technology sector
quiz.explanation: Cash can be a safety buffer or it can be capital that has not been allocated well - you have to read it alongside the capital allocation strategy. Treating it as automatically wasteful ignores the buffer a cyclical business genuinely needs, dismissing the balance entirely ignores the opportunity cost, and there is nothing sector-specific about the question.

quiz.question: A technology company holds an enormous cash pile for years with no investment, no buyback and no M&A. What should an investor ask?
options: Whether the company is definitely about to go bankrupt
Nothing - the cash reserve is no concern of shareholders
Nothing at all, since more cash is always a good thing
Whether management lacks a capital allocation strategy
quiz.explanation: A large cash balance does not create value on its own if there is no clear plan for using it - that capital could have earned a return through reinvestment, been returned to shareholders through buybacks or dividends, or funded value-creating M&A. Holding cash for years with no purpose is a form of hidden opportunity cost, and it is the opposite of a solvency warning.

quiz.question: Why can Treasury and FP&A in the same business look at the same cash figure and recommend different things?
options: Because Treasury guards liquidity while FP&A guards capital efficiency
Because Treasury is not allowed to know the real cash balance
Because one of the two departments is miscalculating the cash figure
Because FP&A only works during the closing stage of the fiscal year
quiz.explanation: This is not a conflict but a natural division of labour: one side protects against risk, the other optimises for value. The business needs both perspectives. Treasury has the fullest view of the cash position of anyone in the company, neither team is working from different numbers, and FP&A runs a planning cycle that continues all year round.

quiz.question: Cash rises steadily for years with no buyback, no M&A and no meaningful capex increase. What does that suggest?
options: The company is certainly preparing to file for bankruptcy soon
This is always a positive signal about financial health
Nothing here is worth an investor's attention at all
The business may lack a clear capital allocation strategy
quiz.explanation: A large cash balance is not automatically bad, but prolonged accumulation with no purpose is a signal worth questioning about management's capital allocation ability. Rising cash is the opposite of the profile a failing company shows, and calling it uniformly positive skips the opportunity cost of capital that is sitting idle instead of earning a return.

quiz.question: Why do companies hold most of their surplus in short-term securities rather than in a current account?
options: Because short-term securities are exempt from corporate income tax
Because accounting standards cap how large a cash balance may be
To pick up some yield while still converting to cash quickly
To avoid disclosing the detailed cash balance in quarterly reports
quiz.explanation: Money sitting still loses value to inflation, but locking it into a long maturity costs you availability. Government bonds and short-dated paper are the middle ground - which is also why this line item is always read together with cash when calculating net debt. There is no tax exemption involved, no accounting ceiling on cash, and the balance is disclosed either way.

keyTakeaways: Treasury and FP&A read cash with different objectives
A large cash balance is not necessarily bad, but there has to be a reason for it
Read it alongside buybacks, capex and M&A

sections.text: The same cash figure on the balance sheet, and yet the Treasury and FP&A functions inside one business ask very different questions about it.
Two perspectives on one cash figure

Treasury cares about liquidity and short-term risk - whether the business has a safe amount of cash for the obligations coming up. FP&A cares about the longer-horizon capital allocation strategy - whether the cash should go to buybacks, M&A, CapEx or reserves. A company holding an enormous cash pile for years with no investment, no buyback and no M&A may be leaving shareholder capital 'buried' in an account rather than creating additional value - a form of hidden opportunity cost.

items: A large cash balance is not automatically a bad signal, provided it comes with a clear capital allocation strategy
But cash left idle for a long time with no purpose is a form of opportunity cost worth worrying about
Read the size of the cash balance alongside the capital allocation decisions: buybacks, capex, M&A

sections.title: Two different questions about the same cash figure

concepts.def: Is there enough cash for near-term obligations? How long could it hold out if revenue were interrupted? Focused on risk, not on yield.
Should the surplus go to reinvestment, share buybacks, M&A, or stay as a buffer? Focused on creating value.

sections.text: How to read a balance sheet with a lot of cash on it

items: Compare cash against annual operating spend to see how long the business would last if revenue stopped entirely - this is Treasury's perspective.
Compare cash against the size of the investment projects available to see whether the business is missing opportunities by holding money too cautiously.
Look at the multi-year trend: is cash rising because it is being accumulated deliberately, or because nobody has an idea for using it?

sections.label: The opportunity cost of idle cash
sections.text: Money left sitting in an account is exposed to inflation and forgoes the chance of a higher return elsewhere. For a fast-growing technology company, every billion held back rather than reinvested in R&D or capacity expansion may be a billion that would have generated an outstanding ROIC - which is why long-term investors tend to ask about the plan for the cash rather than simply being pleased by a large balance.

lines: A large cash figure says nothing on its own.
The more important question is: does the business have a clear plan to turn it into value?

practicePrompt.question: When reading the Cash & Marketable Securities line worth tens of billions of dollars on NVIDIA's financial statements, what does the Treasury function care about most?
options: Liquidity, capital preservation and interest rate risk management
Trading in and out of listed shares to make a quick profit
Buying out all of the smaller competitors in the sector
Holding nothing but physical banknotes locked in a safe
practicePrompt.explanation: The Corporate Treasury function's overriding priorities are Capital Preservation and Liquidity, so that the funding for R&D and for operations is always there.
